Automation Opportunity: - System rule-based auto-approval of "approves promo pricing" (replaces manual Step 3).

Pain Points / Risks: - **Margin erosion from clearance tail**: unsold promotional stock pushed to clearance (W13.9a) often recovers only 40–60% of cost, especially for seasonal hardware items with limited second-use demand
- **POS price override abuse**: cashiers may manually override promotional pricing for favored customers or fail to apply the correct promo price during the transition window

- **Shelf tag timing mismatch**: promotional shelf tags arriving late at provincial stores (Visayas/Mindanao) due to DC delivery schedules means first-day promo sales are missed or incorrect prices displayed

- **Vendor-funded promo disputes**: reconciling vendor-funded markdown reimbursements requires matching POS transaction data to vendor agreement terms — discrepancies of 5–10% are common and delay AP settlement (W7)

- **Promo cannibalization**: aggressive promotional pricing on commodity items (cement, paint) cannibalizes regular-priced sales of adjacent SKUs in the same category, depressing overall category margin
Staffing Implication: - **4 Pricing Analysts**: 6 major promos + 12 monthly cycles = ~18 events/year. Each event requires ~6–8 hours of setup + 30 min/day monitoring during the promo period + 2 hours post-analysis. With staggered events, 4 analysts can handle this alongside regular price maintenance.
System Touchpoints: - Promotional price setup with date-effective pricing (W13.2)
- Approval workflow for promotional prices (W13.3)
- Scheduled push of promo prices to POS (W13.5)
- Auto-application at POS without cashier intervention (W13.7)
- Real-time promo performance dashboard (W13.8)
- Automatic price reversion and clearance flagging (W13.9)
- Post-promo analysis reporting (W13.10)
- Clearance pricing with POS flag and disclaimer enforcement (W13.9a)
- Post-clearance inventory disposition tracking (W13.9b)

- Digital coupon / online promo code management: creation of coupon codes with validity dates, usage limits, and channel restrictions (in-store, online, or both); redemption tracking across channels; synchronization with ecommerce platform (W13.2, W13.5)

- Vendor-funded promotional settlement: for promotions where the vendor funds the markdown (e.g., "buy paint at 20% off, funded by vendor"), system records vendor funding portion per transaction line at POS; accumulates vendor liability in a dedicated promo settlement accrual account; monthly settlement report generated per vendor showing units sold at promo price × vendor share; AP credit memo generated per W7.9b to settle vendor obligation; distinct from W27 (volume-based rebates) — vendor-funded promos are pre-agreed markdown reimbursements tied to specific promotional events

- Pricing conflict resolution rules: (1) If a regular price change (W40) occurs during an active promotion, the promo price is NOT automatically adjusted — promo overrides regular price for the promo period. (2) If a new promotion starts and the regular price has changed since the promo was set up, the system alerts the Pricing Analyst to recalculate the promo price from the new base. (3) If two promotions overlap for the same SKU, system applies the lower price (customer-friendly) and alerts Pricing Analyst to investigate. (4) Post-promotion: system reverts to the CURRENT regular price, not the price active when the promo was created
Time Estimate: ~8–12 hours per major promotional event (setup 4–6 hrs + monitoring 2–3 hrs over promo period + post-analysis 2–3 hrs); ~3–4 hours per monthly hot deal cycle; total ~84–120 hours/year across 4 Pricing Analysts

steps.activity: Buyer receives vendor price increase notice (letter, email, or portal notification); enters new cost and effective date in system
System calculates margin impact: current SRP × current cost vs. current SRP × new cost; shows margin erosion per SKU and total category impact

Pricing Analyst reviews margin impact report; decides action per SKU: (a) absorb cost increase (reduce margin), (b) pass through to SRP, (c) increase SRP partially, (d) negotiate with vendor, (e) switch to alternative vendor, (f) discontinue item
Pricing Analyst enters new SRP per SKU with effective date in system; system shows new margin % for validation
Category Manager reviews and approves price changes; VP Merchandising approves if aggregate margin impact > PHP 500K/month
System schedules price update: new SRP takes effect at configured date/time (typically start of business day)
System pushes updated price file to all POS terminals per nightly sync (or immediately if real-time sync configured); updates ecommerce catalog
Store Operations receives price change bulletin; Department Supervisors update shelf tags before store opening on effective date
System maintains full price history per SKU: date range, old SRP, new SRP, reason code, approver — for audit and BIR compliance
Monthly: Pricing Analyst generates price change summary report: # of changes, average increase/decrease, margin impact, top categories affected

Buyer receives vendor price protection notice: new lower cost with effective date (possibly retroactive); enters in system: vendor, SKU(s), old cost, new cost, effective date, scope (future only vs. retroactive)
If retroactive: system calculates credit due based on quantities purchased between effective date and now; generates vendor credit memo per W7.9b
If on-hand inventory exists at old cost: system revalues on-hand inventory to new cost; posts difference (Dr. Accounts Payable / Cr. COGS or Inventory)
Buyer communicates new cost to Pricing Analyst for SRP review per standard W40 process

Pricing Analyst defines quantity break rules per SKU or category in system: threshold quantity, discount % or fixed price per tier (e.g., cement: 1–9 bags at SRP, 10–99 bags at 5% off, 100+ bags at 8% off); rules are date-effective with start/end dates
Category Manager approves quantity break rules; VP Merchandising approves if aggregate margin impact exceeds threshold
System stores quantity break rules linked to item master; POS automatically applies the correct tier when scanned quantity meets or exceeds threshold — no cashier intervention required

Discount stacking rules: if a promotional price (W13) is lower than the quantity break price, system applies the promo price (customer-friendly) and does not stack discounts; if quantity break price is lower, it applies; trade/corporate account pricing (W5B.4c) and quantity break pricing do not stack — the lower of the two applies

**Loyalty points on discounted transactions**: loyalty points (W17) are earned on the final amount paid by the customer (after all discounts — promotional, quantity break, trade account, price match) but before VAT; this means quantity break discounts reduce the points earned proportionally; PFRS 15 deferred revenue allocation (W17.4) is calculated on the net revenue after all discounts

Monthly: Pricing Analyst reviews quantity break utilization report: frequency of tier triggers by SKU, margin impact, average quantity per transaction for items with quantity breaks, and whether thresholds are driving incremental volume

fields.Frequency: Ongoing (as items are identified); seasonal clearance events ~4–6/year
fields.Participants: Pricing Analyst, Category Manager, Cost Accountant, Store Manager, VP Merchandising
fields.Trigger: Seasonal end-of-cycle clearance; slow-moving inventory identified by W85 (margin analysis) or W1 (assortment review); damaged-but-saleable items from W91; overstock identified by W6 (cycle count) or W31 (demand planning); or product discontinuation (W68)
fields.Volume: ~500–2,000 SKUs per seasonal clearance event; ~50–200 ad-hoc markdowns/month

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-report of "Markdown candidate identification" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-calculate of "calculates markdown price for each candidate SKU" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System rule-based auto-approval of "approves" (replaces manual Step 3).
Background: Markdowns and clearance pricing are distinct from promotional pricing (W13) and product discontinuation (W68). W13 creates temporary price reductions to drive traffic and volume with planned recovery at end of promo. W68 manages the exit of a product from the assortment entirely. Markdowns are permanent price reductions on specific inventory lots to accelerate sell-through of slow-moving, seasonal, or damaged-but-saleable items. Without a dedicated workflow, markdowns are applied inconsistently, margin impact is not tracked, and clearance inventory lingers on shelves consuming valuable retail space. This workflow supports FIN-011 (inventory aging), INV-010 (catch-weight), and W85 (margin analysis).
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: Pricing Analyst review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Premature markdown on seasonal items**: applying markdowns too early on seasonal hardware (e.g., rainy season gear in September) leaves margin on the table when late-season demand spikes from typhoons occur
- **Below-cost authorization delays**: CFO approval for below-cost markdowns (W93.3d) can take 3–5 business days while inventory continues aging and occupying shelf space, deepening the eventual loss

- **Clearance cannibalization of new arrivals**: clearance items displayed near new seasonal merchandise cannibalize full-margin sales, especially in high-traffic categories like paint and power tools

- **Inconsistent escalation execution**: the 2-week / 4-week / 6-week sell-through escalation tiers (W93.6) rely on Pricing Analysts actively reviewing dashboards; missed reviews result in clearance items lingering at insufficient markdown depth

- **Damaged-but-saleable customer perception**: selling cosmetically damaged items (dented cans, scratched tiles) under the BuildRight brand risks eroding quality perception even with clearance disclaimers, particularly in categories where product integrity matters (electrical, plumbing)
Pricing Conflict Rules: - Markdown price vs. promotional price: if an item is on both markdown (W93) and promotion (W13), system applies the **lower** of the two prices at POS (customer-friendly); if the promotional price is higher than markdown, system ignores the promotion
- Markdown price vs. employee discount: employee discount (W5B.12) does **not** stack on top of markdown; the lower of employee discount price or markdown price applies
- Markdown price vs. loyalty points: loyalty points earned on markdown sales calculated on markdown price (not original SRP)
- Markdown price vs. competitor price match (W61): markdown price is the effective SRP for price match comparison
Staffing Implication: - **Pricing Analysts**: add ~4 hours/seasonal clearance event (4 analysts) + ~2 hours/month ad-hoc markdowns. With 4–6 seasonal events/year, this is ~20–30 hours/year incremental. Absorbed.
- **Store Associates**: clearance re-labeling adds ~30 min/store/event × 4–6 events = ~2–3 hours/store/year. Absorbed.
- **No incremental headcount.**
System Touchpoints: - Markdown candidate identification: aging analysis, slow-mover flagging, seasonal calendar integration (W93.1)
- Markdown pricing calculator: WAC floor, markdown % tiers, recovery estimation (W93.2)
- Tiered authorization workflow with amount-based routing (W93.3)
- Markdown price execution: POS and ecommerce price update with original SRP reference preserved (W93.4)
- Clearance shelf label generation per W63 (W93.5)
- Markdown sell-through dashboard with velocity tracking and escalation triggers (W93.6)
- Post-clearance performance analysis with recovery and margin impact reporting (W93.7)
- Pricing conflict rules engine: markdown vs. promo vs. employee discount vs. price match (W93 pricing conflicts)

- Integration with W1 (assortment — slow-mover exit), W13 (promotions — pricing conflict rules), W31 (demand — overstock identification), W40 (price changes — markdown as a permanent price change), W50 (PIM — ecommerce catalog clearance), W63 (shelf labels — clearance tags), W68 (discontinuation — clearance as part of exit), W85 (margin analysis — markdown as margin recovery strategy), W91 (damaged goods — markdown disposition)
Time Estimate: ~4 hours per seasonal clearance event for Pricing Analysts (candidates machine-identified; ~5 min/SKU manual review only on the exception subset); ~30 min/store per event for re-labeling and display setup; ad-hoc markdowns ~2 hours/month; total clearance cycle from identification to post-analysis runs 6–8 weeks

steps.activity: **Markdown candidate identification**: Sources of markdown candidates: (a) **Seasonal clearance**: end-of-season items identified per seasonal calendar (Christmas décor after Dec, flood control after rainy season); (b) **Slow-movers**: SKUs with inventory aging > 90 days and < 2 units sold/month flagged by system from W85 monthly margin report; (c) **Damaged-but-saleable**: items with cosmetic damage but functional per W91 disposition decision (dented cans, box-damaged appliances, scratched tiles); (d) **Overstock**: locations with > 12 weeks of supply vs. forecast per W31; (e) **Near-expiry**: date-sensitive items within 30% of shelf life per W6 near-expiry alerting

**Markdown pricing calculation**: Pricing Analyst calculates markdown price for each candidate SKU: (a) current SRP, (b) current WAC (from inventory valuation), (c) minimum acceptable price (WAC + minimum margin % — configurable per category, typically 0–10% above cost; for clearance, may go below cost with approval), (d) recommended markdown price based on: markdown percentage tiers (25%, 33%, 50%, 75% off SRP), aging velocity (slower movers get deeper markdown), quantity on hand, and weeks of supply; (e) estimated total markdown loss (markdown amount × quantity); (f) estimated recovery value (markdown price × expected sell-through %)

**Authorization** (tiered by markdown value): (a) **≤ PHP 50,000 total markdown loss per SKU**: Category Manager approves; (b) **> PHP 50,000 and ≤ PHP 500,000 total markdown loss**: VP Merchandising approves; (c) **> PHP 500,000 total markdown loss**: CFO approves; (d) **Below-cost markdown**: CFO approval required regardless of amount (loss recognition trigger)

**Markdown execution in system**: (a) Pricing Analyst enters markdown in system with: effective date, markdown price, markdown reason code (seasonal, slow-mover, damaged, overstock, near-expiry), and authorization reference; (b) system updates price in POS (W5B) and ecommerce (W11/W19) — regular SRP preserved as reference; markdown price displayed as "Now" or "Clearance" on shelf label (W63); (c) system posts GL entry: Dr. Markdown Expense (or Dr. COGS-Clearance) / Cr. Inventory — at markdown amount per unit × quantity on hand (if below WAC, recognize loss immediately; if above WAC, no immediate GL impact — margin reduction recognized at sale)

**Shelf label and display update**: (a) System generates clearance shelf labels per W63 with clearance pricing and distinctive visual treatment (e.g., yellow/orange tag); (b) Stock Associate replaces shelf labels at store; (c) for damaged-but-saleable items: Stock Associate moves to designated clearance rack or area with appropriate signage; (d) ecommerce catalog updated with clearance badge and price per W50

**Sell-through monitoring**: (a) System tracks markdown sell-through daily: markdown price × units sold = recovery; remaining markdown inventory × markdown price = remaining recovery; (b) **Escalation tiers**: if < 30% sell-through after 2 weeks: Category Manager reviews — consider deeper markdown; if < 50% sell-through after 4 weeks: Pricing Analyst applies second markdown (additional 25% off) with Level 2 re-authorization; if < 30% sell-through after 6 weeks: proceed to final disposition per W68.9 (RTV, donation, scrap)

**Post-clearance analysis**: After clearance period: Pricing Analyst prepares clearance performance report per event: (a) original markdown value vs. actual recovery, (b) sell-through %, (c) days to clear, (d) margin impact by category, (e) lessons learned (markdown timing, depth, vendor quality issues); feeds into W85 annual margin strategy and W1 assortment decisions

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-log of "log review" (replaces manual Step 1).

Background: BuildRight operates 5+ concurrent pricing mechanisms: regular SRP (W40), promotional pricing (W13), trade/corporate account pricing (W5B.4c, W24), quantity break pricing (W40.15–19), competitor price matching (W61), and employee discount (W5B.12). Each has its own workflow, but there is no unified governance framework defining the pricing rule hierarchy (which price wins when multiple prices apply), periodic compliance verification (are shelf tags, POS, and ecommerce prices aligned?), and audit of pricing override patterns. This workflow creates that governance layer.

Background: W40 handles scheduled regular price changes (typically weekly or monthly cycles). W61 handles individual customer price matches at the store level. W13 handles promotional pricing execution. However, none of these address the need for a rapid, coordinated response to a competitive price move that threatens BuildRight's market position. In Philippine hardware retail, major competitors (e.g., national retail chains or local players) may launch unscheduled price cuts on key items. BuildRight needs a defined process to evaluate the threat, decide on a response, and execute it across all affected channels within 24–48 hours — far faster than the standard W40 cycle.
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: VP Merchandising review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Margin erosion from price wars** — a tactical response to one competitor's price cut may trigger a chain reaction where multiple competitors continue undercutting, resulting in a race to the bottom with permanent margin damage

- **Execution speed vs. accuracy trade-off** — the 24–48 hour response window means price impact assessment is necessarily quick and may underestimate margin effects, especially on slow-moving SKUs where demand elasticity data is thin

- **Channel inconsistency risk**: if POS prices update within 1 hour but shelf labels take 24 hours, customers see different prices on the shelf vs. at the register, creating confusion and complaints; mitigated by the VP Merchandising review and approval gate

- **Competitive intelligence reliability** — W130 data is only as good as the intelligence gathering process; if competitor prices are misreported, BuildRight may respond to a non-existent threat, sacrificing margin unnecessarily
Staffing Implication: - **Pricing Analyst**: primary driver of tactical responses; ~11–15 hours per response × 2–4 responses/month = ~22–60 hours/month. At 2–4 events/month, this can consume 15–40% of a Pricing Analyst's capacity during competitive peaks. Absorbed within existing Merchandising team.
- **Category Manager**: ~3–4 hours per response for impact assessment and options development. With 2–4 events/month across categories, this is shared across multiple Category Managers. Absorbed.
- **VP Merchandising**: ~1 hour per response for decision-making. Absorbed within existing leadership duties.
- **Marketing Manager**: ~2–4 hours per response for campaign support. Absorbed.
- **No incremental headcount.**
System Touchpoints: - Competitor price intelligence feed (W130) integrated with pricing master (W289) for automated alert generation when competitor price deviates beyond threshold (W329.1)
- Price elasticity analytics: historical sales response to price changes by category and SKU (W329.2)

Time Estimate: Threat assessment (steps 1–2): 1.5–2.5 hours. Response development and approval (steps 3–4): 1.5–2.5 hours. Execution (steps 5–6): 2.5–4.5 hours. Monitoring (step 7): 15 min/day × 14 days = 3.5 hours. Post-mortem (step 8): 2 hours. **Total per tactical response: ~11–15 hours over 30 days.**

steps.activity: **Threat identification and alert**: W130 competitor price intelligence feed flags significant competitive price changes; Pricing Analyst reviews alerts and classifies threat level: (a) **Low** — isolated SKU, no pattern, no response needed, (b) **Medium** — multiple SKUs in a category affected, potential customer traffic impact, (c) **High** — competitor campaign on core categories (cement, paint, lumber), threatensBuildRight's price positioning

**Impact assessment**: For Medium and High threats: Category Manager analyzes: (a) sales velocity of affected SKUs (revenue impact if customers switch to competitor), (b) current margin on affected SKUs (room to cut), (c) inventory position (how much stock is at risk of becoming dead if we don't respond), (d) historical price elasticity for the category, (e) competitive context — is this a temporary promo or permanent price change?

**Response options development**: Pricing Analyst and Category Manager prepare response options: (a) **Match price** — reduce BuildRight price to match competitor (margin sacrifice), (b) **Selective match** — match on top 10–20 traffic-driving SKUs only, maintain regular price on remainder, (c) **Value-add response** — keep price but bundle with free delivery, extended warranty, or loyalty bonus points, (d) **No response** — absorb the competitive threat if margin impact is unacceptable; each option includes projected margin impact, revenue impact, and inventory risk

**Decision and approval**: VP Merchandising selects response strategy; for margin impact > PHP 500K/month or price reduction > 15% on any SKU: CEO approval required; for margin impact ≤ PHP 500K/month: VP Merchandising approves; decision documented with rationale in system

**Price execution**: Pricing Analyst executes approved price changes in pricing master (W289); system propagates: (a) updated prices to POS (within 60 seconds per POS-047), (b) updated prices to ecommerce (within 5 minutes per NFR SLA), (c) updated prices to marketplace channels (W180) if affected SKUs are listed, (d) generates updated shelf labels for stores (W63, W181) — stores receive label reprint instruction with next-day printing deadline

**Marketing support**: If response includes promotional positioning ("Price Match Guarantee" or "Lowest Price" messaging), Marketing Manager activates pre-approved tactical campaign assets: in-store signage, social media posts, email/SMS to loyalty members; Marketing coordinates with W83 campaign workflow for customer-facing communication

**Monitoring and exit**: Pricing Analyst monitors affected SKU sales daily for 14 days post-response: (a) sales volume vs. pre-response baseline, (b) margin impact vs. projection, (c) competitor behavior — have they further reduced prices or returned to normal? At day 14: VP Merchandising decides whether to maintain tactical pricing, transition to permanent price change (W40), or restore original pricing

**Post-mortem**: At day 30, Category Manager prepares tactical response post-mortem: actual vs. projected margin impact, sales volume change, market share assessment (qualitative from W130 data), lessons learned; feeds into quarterly pricing strategy review (W107)

Background: W93 covers markdown and clearance pricing execution at the operational level. This workflow adds the analytics and optimization layer: using data-driven methods to determine the optimal markdown timing, depth, and cadence that maximizes recovery value while clearing aging inventory. For a PHP 62.3B revenue retailer with 35,000 SKUs, even a 1% improvement in markdown recovery translates to ~PHP 50-100M in annual margin improvement. This workflow complements W220 (SLOB provisioning) by addressing the upstream optimization question: what is the best markdown strategy for each item?
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: Pricing Analyst review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Markdown depth uncertainty**: pricing elasticity varies significantly by category and season; over-markdown erodes margin, under-markdown leaves inventory unsold
- **Vendor markdown conflicts**: vendor-funded inventory may require vendor approval for markdown, causing delays in markdown execution while inventory ages further
- **Customer perception damage**: frequent or deep markdowns can train customers to wait for sales rather than buy at full price, eroding full-price sell-through

- **Cross-channel markdown consistency**: maintaining the same markdown price across POS, ecommerce, and marketplace channels per W678 is operationally complex when each channel has different markdown execution timelines
Staffing Implication: Pricing Analyst: ~4–8 hours/week on markdown optimization analytics. Category Manager: ~30–60 min/week on approval decisions. Absorbed within existing Merchandising team. No incremental headcount.
System Touchpoints: - Inventory aging analytics per INV-011

Time Estimate: **Weekly cycle**: 5-9 hours (1-2 hours candidate identification + 2-4 hours optimization + 30-60 min approval + 1-2 hours performance tracking).

steps.activity: **Weekly markdown candidate identification**: Pricing Analyst runs weekly markdown candidate report: (a) criteria for markdown consideration: (i) inventory age >90 days for seasonal items, >180 days for non-seasonal; (ii) sell-through rate <50% of forecast; (iii) weeks of supply >26 weeks (6 months); (iv) SLOB items identified per W220; (v) items approaching end-of-season per W264; (b) for each candidate: current inventory value, weeks of supply, sell-through rate trend, margin at current price, category priority

**Markdown optimization analysis**: for each candidate SKU, Pricing Analyst determines optimal markdown: (a) historical markdown response analysis: how did similar items respond to markdowns in past seasons?; (b) price elasticity estimation: at what markdown depth does sell-through accelerate sufficiently?; (c) recovery value optimization: markdown % × projected sell-through = recovery value; find markdown % that maximizes recovery; (d) timing optimization: is it better to mark down now or wait for end-of-season clearance?; (e) cadence: single deep markdown vs. staged markdown (e.g., 20% → 30% → 50% over 6 weeks); (f) present recommendations to Category Manager with supporting data

**Markdown approval and execution**: Category Manager approves markdown strategy: (a) verify markdown does not violate vendor price protection agreements per W161; (b) verify vendor consent if markdown affects vendor-funded inventory; (c) confirm markdown aligns with overall margin plan per W102 category P&L; (d) approved markdowns entered into pricing system per W40 for execution; (e) execution at store level per W93 (markdown & clearance pricing execution); (f) ecommerce price sync per W678 multi-channel pricing consistency

**Markdown performance tracking**: weekly, Pricing Analyst tracks markdown performance: (a) for each active markdown: (i) sell-through rate since markdown activation; (ii) remaining inventory and weeks of supply; (iii) actual recovery value vs. projected; (b) identify underperforming markdowns: items not clearing as projected → accelerate to deeper markdown or activate clearance per W532; (c) identify overperforming markdowns: items clearing too fast → potential markdown was too deep, learn for future; (d) final disposition for remaining clearance items: donate per W552, liquidate to jobbers, or dispose per W91

Background: W513 covers vendor-funded promotional activity and co-op advertising management. W27 covers vendor rebate accrual and settlement. This workflow addresses the broader trade fund management discipline: negotiating, tracking, and reconciling the promotional funding that vendors provide to BuildRight for in-store promotions, advertising, display placement, and co-marketing activities. For a PHP 62.3B retailer where the top 20 vendors account for ~45% of COGS, trade funds represent a significant financial flow (~PHP 500M-1B annually) that requires disciplined tracking to ensure BuildRight maximizes vendor funding and vendors receive agreed-upon promotional support.
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: Trade Marketing Manager review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Proof-of-performance disputes**: vendors frequently dispute whether BuildRight executed agreed promotional activities as specified (ad placement, display size, timing), requiring extensive documentation to support deductions

- **Trade fund underutilization**: BuildRight may fail to utilize all available vendor trade funds within the agreement period, leaving money on the table and weakening negotiating position for next year
- **Accrual vs. cash timing mismatch**: trade funds are accrued based on purchase volume but consumed by promotional activities that may occur months later, creating reconciliation complexity
- **Vendor perception of unfairness**: vendors may perceive that BuildRight prioritizes its own margin over jointly agreed promotional objectives, straining the vendor relationship
Staffing Implication: Trade Marketing Manager: ~8–12 hours/month on trade fund management. Category Managers: ~4–6 hours/month on fund allocation decisions. Finance Manager: ~4–6 hours/month on reconciliation. No incremental headcount.

steps.activity: **Annual trade fund negotiation**: during annual joint business planning per W155: (a) Category Manager and Trade Marketing Manager negotiate trade fund commitments with each top-20 vendor: (i) annual trade fund amount (typically 2-5% of projected annual purchases); (ii) fund allocation by activity: in-store promotions, co-op advertising, display fees, new product launch support, seasonal campaigns; (iii) fund accrual method: lump sum, quarterly accrual based on purchases, or per-event; (iv) fund utilization criteria: what activities qualify, documentation requirements, proof-of-performance; (v) fund expiration: unused funds at year-end — carried forward or forfeited; (b) document agreed terms in trade fund agreement per W402 contract master; (c) Finance reviews fund terms for margin impact per W85

**Promotional event fund commitment**: when promotional event is planned per W83: (a) Trade Marketing Manager identifies which vendors should contribute based on: (i) products featured in the promotion; (ii) vendor trade fund balance available; (iii) historical vendor contribution for similar events; (b) calculate vendor contribution: (i) co-op advertising share: % of media spend allocated to vendor's products; (ii) in-store display cost: fixture, signage, and space allocation; (iii) promotional markdown funding: vendor's share of promotional price reduction; (c) obtain vendor agreement on contribution amount per W513 vendor-funded promotional activity; (d) book commitment against vendor's trade fund balance in system

**Monthly trade fund reconciliation**: Finance Manager and Trade Marketing Manager reconcile monthly: (a) for each vendor with active trade fund: (i) opening fund balance; (ii) additions: new accruals from purchases during the month; (iii) deductions: commitments for promotional activities, co-op advertising, display costs, markdown funding; (iv) proof-of-performance documentation: did the promotional activity actually occur? Were the agreed terms met?; (v) closing fund balance; (b) resolve discrepancies: (i) vendor disputes BuildRight's deduction: provide proof-of-performance documentation; (ii) BuildRight identifies underfunded activity: negotiate additional vendor contribution; (iii) unused fund balance approaching expiration: propose utilization plan; (c) reconciliation shared with vendor for agreement

**Quarterly trade fund effectiveness review**: Category Manager reviews trade fund ROI quarterly: (a) for each vendor's trade fund: (i) total vendor funding received; (ii) incremental sales generated by vendor-funded promotions; (iii) incremental margin after deducting BuildRight's execution cost; (iv) ROI = incremental margin / vendor funding; (b) benchmark vendors: which vendors provide the highest trade fund ROI?; (c) identify underperforming trade fund allocations: redirect to higher-ROI activities in next negotiation; (d) insights feed into next annual negotiation per W155 JBP

**Year-end trade fund settlement**: at fiscal year-end: (a) Finance Manager conducts final reconciliation for all vendor trade funds: (i) total accrued vs. total utilized vs. total remaining; (b) for unused funds: (i) if agreement allows carry-forward: roll balance to next year; (ii) if funds expire: negotiate with vendor for extension or reallocation; (iii) if funds are non-refundable credits: apply against AP balance per W7; (c) prepare year-end trade fund summary for each vendor; (d) archive all documentation per W256 retention policy

Background: BuildRight Depot carries construction materials (cement, steel rebar, lumber, copper wire, PVC pipe) whose input commodity prices fluctuate weekly in Philippine markets. Cement prices are influenced by energy costs and seasonal demand spikes during dry season. Steel rebar tracks global iron ore prices with a lag. Lumber prices vary by import costs and seasonal typhoon-driven demand. Unlike stable-consumer-price retail categories, these construction commodities can see 5–15% price swings within a month. Without systematic monitoring and dynamic adjustment, BuildRight either erodes margins (selling at old prices while cost has risen) or loses sales (pricing above market when cost drops). With 55% of revenue from B2C and 30% from B2B trade/contractor customers who are price-sensitive and well-informed, price competitiveness on core construction materials is a strategic imperative. Philippine hardware retail competitors (CTHI, Wilcon, etc.) adjust prices frequently; BuildRight must match.
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: Pricing Analyst review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Speed of adjustment** — commodity prices can spike rapidly (e.g., cement shortage after typhoon); if weekly cadence is too slow, BuildRight sells at a loss for days; consider threshold-based trigger for emergency price adjustments outside weekly cycle
- **Competitive intelligence lag** — competitor prices are manually gathered per W130; during rapid market shifts, BuildRight may not know if competitors have already adjusted

- **Store shelf label compliance** — price changes propagate to POS instantly but shelf labels require manual update; customers seeing wrong price on shelf but charged different at POS creates complaints and DTI compliance risk per W468

- **Trade account pricing impact** — construction material price volatility affects B2B trade account pricing differently than B2C; trade price adjustments must be communicated to account holders proactively
Staffing Implication: - Pricing Analyst: ~6 hours/week dedicated to volatile SKU monitoring (absorbed by existing 4 Pricing Analyst roles). No incremental headcount.

- W63 shelf label distribution for physical label updates

- W107 pricing hierarchy governance for approval authority
- W13 promotions execution for promo price interaction rules
- W31 demand forecasting for demand elasticity integration
- POS event streaming for near-real-time price propagation
- Ecommerce platform for online price sync

steps.activity: **Weekly commodity price intake**: Pricing Analyst receives vendor price bulletins, monitors DTI Suggested Retail Price advisories for cement, and tracks commodity indices (steel, copper)

**Price adjustment recommendation**: Generate price adjustment proposal: (a) SKUs requiring SRP increase (cost up, margin below floor); (b) SKUs requiring SRP decrease (cost down, price uncompetitive); (c) hold recommendations (within tolerance band); (d) impact on loyalty pricing, trade pricing, and corporate contract pricing per W40

Background: The Philippine home improvement retail market is increasingly competitive, with regional players (CitiHardware, Wilcon Depot, Montalbo) and local hardware stores competing on price for commoditized items (cement, nails, paint, electrical supplies). BuildRight Depot operates 200 stores across diverse markets where local pricing dynamics vary significantly. Department Supervisors are the "eyes on the ground" for competitor pricing intelligence, feeding data to HQ Pricing Analysts who adjust pricing strategy per category and region. This workflow ensures BuildRight maintains competitive positioning while protecting margin.
Controls: - CTL-241 (ensure controlled execution — Pricing & Promotions (PA-01.2).)
- operational: Pricing Analyst review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Data quality inconsistency** — Department Supervisors may record competitor prices for different pack sizes, grades, or brands, making direct comparison unreliable; standardized SKU mapping and photo evidence requirements mitigate but add friction

- **Competitor response escalation** — aggressive price matching can trigger price wars, especially with local hardware stores who have lower overhead; margin erosion risk if price actions are reactive rather than strategic; mitigated by the Pricing Analyst review and approval gate

- **Observation burden** — adding 30 min/week of competitor monitoring to Department Supervisors already managing a heavy daily workflow load; risk of data quality decline if perceived as low priority; mitigated by the Pricing Analyst review and approval gate

- **Regional pricing complexity** — competitor landscapes vary dramatically across 200 stores; a single national price for commodities like cement may be uncompetitive in some regions while leaving money on the table in others
Staffing Implication: - **Department Supervisors**: ~50 min/week per store (4 Supervisors × ~12.5 min each). Absorbed by existing role.
- **Pricing Analysts**: ~7 hours/week on competitive analysis and reporting. Absorbed by existing 4 Pricing Analysts.
- **Category Managers**: ~2 hours/week on price action decisions. Absorbed by existing role.
- **No incremental headcount.**

steps.activity: **Competitor identification per store**: Each Department Supervisor maintains a list of 3–5 key local competitors within 5 km radius; competitor profile includes: store name, format (big-box vs. talipapa vs. specialty), key overlapping categories, and general pricing positioning (discount vs. premium)

**Weekly price observation**: Department Supervisors observe competitor shelf prices or promotional flyers for a rotating category list assigned by Pricing Analyst (e.g., Week 1: cement & lumber, Week 2: paint & electrical, Week 3: tools & hardware); record 25–30 key item prices via mobile app with photo evidence where possible

**Mobile app data submission**: Department Supervisor enters competitor prices into the Competitor Price Intelligence mobile app: (a) select competitor, (b) scan or manually enter BuildRight SKU, (c) enter competitor price, (d) note promotional context (regular, sale, clearance), (e) attach photo if available; data synced to central pricing database

**Automated competitive analysis**: System matches competitor prices against BuildRight current SRP: (a) calculates price gap (% above/below BuildRight), (b) flags items where BuildRight is >10% above competitor (price risk), (c) flags items where BuildRight is >20% below competitor (margin opportunity), (d) generates competitive positioning heatmap by region and category

**Weekly price intelligence report**: Pricing Analyst reviews system-generated competitive analysis: (a) identifies categories where BuildRight is losing on price in specific regions, (b) identifies categories where BuildRight can increase price without competitive risk, (c) drafts price adjustment recommendations with margin impact estimate, (d) presents to Category Manager

**Price action decisions**: Category Manager reviews recommendations and decides: (a) match competitor price (markdown per W93), (b) maintain current price with value proposition differentiation (brand, service, availability), (c) adjust trade pricing for B2B accounts in affected region per W112, (d) trigger promotional response per W262; VP Merchandising approves changes above PHP 50,000 impact per SKU

**Monthly market intelligence briefing**: Pricing Analyst compiles monthly competitive landscape report for VP Merchandising: (a) competitor expansion activity (new store openings, renovations), (b) category-level price trends, (c) emerging local competitors, (d) vendor-exclusive deals observed at competitors; feeds into quarterly category strategy review per W1
